rules.title: Jersey City Rent Control Ordinance (Chapter 260)
rules.requirement: Jersey City regulates residential rents through its Rent Control Ordinance, Chapter 260 of the Municipal Code. The Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations administers and enforces it, and a Rent Leveling Board hears matters under it. Landlords may apply for rent increases above the regulated rent through three applications: capital improvement, vacancy capital improvement and hardship. Tenants may file an Illegal Rent Petition or a Failure to Maintain Service Petition seeking a rent reduction. All properties with 1-4 units are exempt. Owners may submit a Rent Control Exemption Request for other exemptions the ordinance permits. The captured source does not state the annual cap or formula. It links a Consumer Price Index chart but gives no figure.

unverifiable_exemptions: Other exemptions permitted by Chapter 260, available through a Rent Control Exemption Request reviewed by the Office (criteria not stated in the captured source)
coverage.summary: Covers rental properties with 5 or more units. All 1-4 unit properties are exempt. Further exemptions are available on request if the owner meets the ordinance's criteria.
coverage.other_conditions: Further exemptions may be granted on an owner's Rent Control Exemption Request if the property meets the ordinance's criteria.

rules.exemptions: All 1-4 unit properties. Other exemptions permitted by the ordinance may be granted on a Rent Control Exemption Request; the captured source does not detail them.
rules.effective_date_note: The captured source gives no enactment or effective date for Chapter 260. The ordinance is administered as current law (Rent Leveling Board calendar 2026).
rules.quoted_span: All 1-4 Unit Properties are exempt from rent control
rules.review_note: This record rests on the official Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations webpage, not on the ordinance text. Four items still need checking against Chapter 260 itself: the cap formula (the page links a CPI chart), the section-level citation, the full list of exemptions, and any new-construction exemption. New Jersey has no statewide rent cap; the state Anti-Eviction Act requires rent increases to comply with municipal rent control.
rules.source_notes: Two candidates drawn from the same official city webpage (D036) were merged.

rules.title: Preventing Algorithmic Rent-Fixing in the Rental Housing Market (Jersey City Code § 218-12, as amended by Ord. 25-076)
rules.requirement:
A real estate lessor, agent or subcontractor may not do any of the following with a Service Provider:
- subscribe to its services
- contract with it
- exchange anything of value for its services
- otherwise use its services (wording added by Ord. 25-076)

A Service Provider is any person that performs a coordinating function for a real estate lessor. Coordinating has three elements:
- collecting nonpublic competitor information from lessors, or collecting historical or current prices, price changes, supply levels, occupancy rates, or lease termination and renewal dates from two or more lessors or from public databases
- analyzing that information with a computational system, software or process
- recommending rental prices, lease terms or occupancy levels to a lessor

Nonpublic Competitor Information is material lease information less than 365 days old that is not widely and readily available to the public at no cost.

No service provider may facilitate an agreement not to compete among lessors on rental pricing, fees or any other rental terms.

Public enforcement may be brought as parens patriae by the Attorney General or by any municipal or county attorney. The Office of Landlord-Tenant Affairs and the Office of Code Compliance may enforce the section. Complaints are compiled by the Office of Landlord/Tenant Relations, which may investigate them or refer them for prosecution.

Any injured person has a private right of action. Successful plaintiffs, including government enforcers, recover costs and reasonable attorney fees.
rules.key_value: First violation punishable under Jersey City Code § 1-25. Subsequent violations: fine of $100 to $2,000. Each day of violation is a separate violation. Private right of action with costs and attorney fees.

coverage.summary: Applies to real estate lessors of residential dwelling units in Jersey City, meaning units intended as a person's primary residence. Also applies to their agents and subcontractors and to service providers. Inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care and detention or correctional facilities are excluded. No unit-count or building-age limits.
coverage.owner_conditions: The definition of coordination exempts owners of multiple properties for actions related exclusively to properties controlled by the same rental property owner.
coverage.other_conditions: Licensed real estate agents are excluded from the coordination and service-provider definitions while operating in accordance with all applicable state regulations.

rules.exemptions: Actions by an owner of multiple properties relating exclusively to properties it controls. Licensed real estate agents operating in accordance with state regulations. Inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities are not residential dwelling units.
rules.effective_date_note: Neither ordinance states an effective date. Ord. 25-057 was adopted on final reading on May 21, 2025 and approved by the Mayor on May 22, 2025. Ord. 25-076 amended § 218-12(2); it was adopted on July 16, 2025 and approved by the Mayor on July 17, 2025. A secondary law-firm table (DX06) gives 'effective June 2025' (month only). That is consistent with the May 2025 adoption, but the exact date is unconfirmed by an official source. The section is in force as of the query date either way.

rules.quoted_span:
It is unlawful for any real estate lessor, agent, or subcontractor thereof, to subscribe to, contract with, or otherwise
exchange anything of value in return for the services of a Service Provider.
rules.conflict_note: Organizer open question: New Jersey's FAIR Act (P.L.2026, c.43; effective July 1, 2027) may preempt this ordinance once it takes effect. Its section 6(b) prohibits municipal ordinances that conflict with the act. The ordinance differs from the act in its definitions, penalties and private right of action, and whether those differences amount to a conflict is unresolved.
rules.review_note: The § 1-25 penalty for a first violation is not reproduced in the captured documents. The ordinance text calls Chapter 218 both 'Multiple Dwellings' and 'Fees and Charges'. It also refers to 'this Act' and 'this chapter'. It renumbers the existing §§ 218-12 to 218-18 as §§ 218-13 to 218-19.
rules.source_notes: The primary source is the adopted base ordinance (DX02, Ord. 25-057). The amending ordinance DX04 (Ord. 25-076) added 'or otherwise utilize' to § 218-12(2)(a); it was merged here as the same law. The Hudson County View article (DX11) describes the 9-0 passage and says further amendments might follow. Those remarks are resolved by the July 2025 amendment. The article's question about excluding Multiple Listing Services is not reflected in either ordinance's text. The $2,000 daily figure cited by a commenter (DX11) and by the law-firm table (DX06) matches the ordinance's subsequent-violation maximum, with each day a separate violation.
